core_principles: The push-up is an upper-extremity weight-bearing exercise that can improve joint stability and proprioception through joint compression forces.
In both traditional and modified (knees-down) push-ups, the percentage of body mass supported is lower in the 'up' position compared to the 'down' position.
The pattern of resistance in push-ups is influenced by the moment arms between the support surface contact point (knees or feet) and the hands.
Adjusting the range of motion can help accommodate strength differences in beginners and clients rehabilitating from injury.
specific_findings: Study analyzed twenty-eight highly strength-trained male subjects.
Force was measured using a force platform in 4 static positions: the up and down positions for both traditional and modified push-ups.
The percentage change in percent body mass supported from the up to the down position was greater in the modified push-up variant than in the traditional push-up.

core_principles: Overall muscle activation of the prime movers increases as the push-up variant becomes more intense.
The activation pattern of upper-extremity synergists, scapular, and trunk stabilizers depends on hand position, joint angles, and the support surface.
Maintain a rigid spine and lower-extremity segments throughout the movement.
Position hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, centered under the shoulders.
Maintain an angle of approximately 180 degrees between the upper and lower body.
common_mistakes: Performing a push-up with the forearm in 90 degrees of internal rotation, which increases posterior and varus elbow shear forces.
Failing to maintain a rigid spine and lower-extremity alignment.
specific_findings: Lou reported the greatest posterior and varus elbow shear forces while performing a push-up with the forearm in 90 degrees of internal rotation.
Donkers reported elbow axial forces during the traditional push-up in a range of 37 to 45% of body mass (BM).
The study evaluated 28 highly strength-trained male subjects (mean age 33.62 +/- 8.59 years, mean BM 84.66 +/- 11.65 kg, mean height 178.98 +/- 5.76 cm).
Gouvali and Boudolos reported that the peak ground reaction force (GRF) over the full range of motion (ROM) in the traditional push-up was significantly higher than in the knees-down variation.

core_principles: Rest at least 1 minute between trials or sets to minimize the effects of fatigue on performance.
Analyze vertical forces as a percentage of body mass (BM) to understand load distribution in different push-up variants.
specific_findings: The study involved a sample size of 28 subjects.
Mean vertical forces were calculated and averaged over 3 trials in each position and expressed as a percentage of the subject's body mass (BM).

core_principles: Traditional push-ups require supporting a significantly higher percentage of body mass compared to modified (knee) push-ups.
For both traditional and modified push-up variations, the percentage of body mass supported is greater in the down position than in the up position.
Modifying a push-up to the knees reduces the relative load on the upper body, making it an effective regression for strength progression.
specific_findings: In the traditional push-up, subjects supported 69.16% (+/- 2.83%) of their body mass in the up position.
In the traditional push-up, subjects supported 75.04% (+/- 2.62%) of their body mass in the down position.
In the modified push-up, subjects supported 53.56% (+/- 4.27%) of their body mass in the up position.
In the modified push-up, subjects supported 61.80% (+/- 3.48%) of their body mass in the down position.
The study analyzed a sample size of 28 subjects, yielding a statistical power of 0.98.
A significant type by position interaction was found: F[1,27] = 18.42, p < 0.001.

core_principles: A greater proportion of body mass is supported in the down position of a push-up compared to the up position for both traditional and modified variations.
Traditional push-ups require supporting a significantly greater percentage of body mass than modified (knees-down) push-ups in both the up and down positions.
The relative change in body mass supported from the up to the down position is significantly greater in the modified push-up than in the traditional push-up.
The increased force in the down position is a consequence of the whole-body center of mass being located further from the point of contact (feet or knees) with the floor, resulting in greater torque.
Traditional push-ups result in greater electromyography (EMG) activity in the pectoralis major and triceps brachii compared to modified push-ups.
Muscle activation of the upper extremity (including pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, posterior deltoid, and infraspinatus) increases proportionally with increased weight-bearing demands.
common_mistakes: Assuming that the percentage of body mass supported remains constant throughout the entire range of motion of a push-up.
Underestimating the relative increase in load/torque experienced at the bottom (down) position of both traditional and modified push-ups.
specific_findings: The percent change in body mass (BM) supported from the up to the down position in traditional push-ups was 8.59 +/- 3.77%.
The percent change in body mass (BM) supported from the up to the down position in modified push-ups was 15.76 +/- 7.03%.
Gouvali and Boudolos (10) reported peak vertical ground reaction forces (GRFs) equal to 66% BM over the traditional push-up ROM and 53% BM over the modified push-up ROM.
Donkers et al. (7) reported axial elbow joint reaction forces of 37% and 38% BW in the up and down positions of the traditional push-up, respectively.
Statistical analysis showed significant differences in BM supported in traditional (F[1,27] = 24276.07, p < 0.001) and modified (F[1,27] = 7493.69, p < 0.001) variants between up and down positions.

core_principles: Traditional push-up with a plus (including scapular protraction at the top of the ROM) preferentially activates the serratus anterior over the upper trapezius.
Performing a push-up with a plus results in high activation of the upper and lower subscapularis and infraspinatus muscles.
Wall push-ups result in a high upper trapezius to serratus anterior activation ratio, which may be less desirable for scapular positioning rehabilitation.
Increased weight-bearing in the upper extremities increases the activation of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles for glenohumeral stabilization.

Traditional push-ups are highly effective for strengthening rotator cuff muscles, while modified push-ups are excellent for targeting the serratus anterior and optimizing the upper trapezius/serratus anterior ratio.

The resistance curve of a push-up is opposite to the human strength curve: the highest percentage of body weight is supported at the bottom (down position) where human pressing strength is lowest, and the lowest percentage is supported at the top (up position) where strength is highest.
For beginners or rehabilitation patients, modifying the range of motion (ROM) may be necessary to accommodate strength limitations at the bottom of the movement.

The modified push-up features a greater proportional increase in the percentage of body mass supported from the up to the down position compared to the traditional push-up due to torso angles and center of mass moment arms.
common_mistakes: Using wall push-ups when trying to target the serratus anterior, as it results in an undesirably high upper trapezius/serratus anterior ratio.

Failing to adjust or shorten the range of motion for beginners or rehab patients, which can overload them at the bottom of the movement (the sticking point) where strength is lowest but load is highest.
specific_findings: The highest force in upper-extremity pressing is exerted near full extension of the elbows, at an angle of approximately 120 degrees.
A paired t-test indicated a signiﬁcantly greater increase in the percentage of BM supported in the modiﬁed than in the traditional push-up variant from the up to the down position.
The modiﬁed push-up is characterized by a lower arm elevation level and a smaller weight-bearing demand but equivalent serratus anterior activation, as compared to the push-up with a plus exercise.
The wall push-up resulted in a higher upper trapezius/serratus anterior ratio compared with that in the traditional push-up.

core_principles: Be cognizant of the relatively greater change in resistance over the full range of motion (ROM) in closed-chain exercises.
In the early stages of post-surgical shoulder rehabilitation, the demand on the serratus anterior muscle at the bottom of the ROM during a modified push-up may be too high.
High demand at the bottom of the ROM can lead to altered scapular kinematics.
Ensure close monitoring of the trainee to maintain correct execution, particularly at the bottom of the ROM, even though the modified push-up is lower intensity than the traditional push-up.
common_mistakes: Altered scapular kinematics at the bottom of the range of motion (ROM).
Incorrect execution or loss of form at the bottom of the ROM due to excessive demand on the serratus anterior.

core_principles: The modified push-up is an effective alternative for individuals unable to perform a traditional push-up and is ideal for early-stage weight-bearing rehabilitation.
The modified push-up helps optimize the strength ratio between the upper trapezius and serratus anterior, promoting scapulothoracic stability.
The traditional push-up is more demanding and applies increased forces, making it more effective for strengthening prime movers, rotator cuff muscles, and regaining glenohumeral joint stability.
When incorporating push-ups into rehabilitation, the range of motion (ROM) may need to be altered to prevent putting undue stress on weak or injured structures.
While overall resistance is lower in a modified push-up, the change in resistance is greater over the ROM compared to a traditional push-up.
common_mistakes: Failing to alter the range of motion (ROM) for injured patients, which can place undue stress on weak or healing structures.
Progressing to the traditional push-up before establishing adequate scapulothoracic stability using the modified push-up.
specific_findings: The subjects in this study were highly resistance-trained males.
Although the overall resistance is lower in a modified push-up compared with a traditional push-up, the change in resistance is greater over the ROM.

core_principles: Abdominal muscles are the primary contributors to maintaining vertebral joint stiffness during the push-up.
specific_findings: Abdominal muscles dominate contributions to vertebral joint stiffness during the push-up (Howarth, Beach, & Callaghan, 2008).

core_principles: Scapular stabilizing synergists can be targeted and analyzed through specific push-up progressions.
Unstable support surfaces, such as Swiss balls, are utilized in research to evaluate changes in scapulothoracic stabilizing muscle activity during push-up and push-up plus variations.
Forearm rotation during the push-up exercise influences the biomechanical load experienced by the elbow.
The relative activation ratio of the serratus anterior and upper trapezius is a critical metric for shoulder rehabilitation and exercise selection.
Range of motion (full vs. partial) is a key variable in strength development and joint action duration during pressing movements.
